toc.title: How I work: from the top of the funnel down
"Activate and relax at the same time"
What helps someone enter their safety state
The answer: you need your safety state, not exactly relaxation

blocks.p: Do you need to relax in order to discharge trauma, or do you need to discharge trauma in order to relax? The answer is kind of both, and I'll explain why.
A reader left a comment on my blog post "Polyvagal Safety and How To Use It." It's a little longer, so I'll take it in chunks. Here's how it started:

q: Hi there. I've been through the trauma therapy mill, and I'm not sure what to do now. I've seen three SE therapists who unfortunately haven't been able to help me.

blocks.p: SE is Somatic Experiencing. People credentialed in Somatic Experiencing are not necessarily therapists. A therapist, a psychotherapist, is someone who is licensed in their state. That's the way it works in the United States, at least; I'm not sure about every other country or governing body. Each state has its own licensing and schooling standards.

Somatic Experiencing as a modality has its own standards, but that's distinct from being a licensed therapist. A therapist can be trained in Somatic Experiencing and become an SE practitioner. That's actually something I'm pretty interested in. But an SE practitioner can be that on their own, without a psychotherapy license. So "three SE therapists" might not mean three licensed psychotherapists. Maybe they are, but they could also be Somatic Experiencing practitioners.
The comment goes on:

q: My body is stuck in a pattern of activation which causes me an extraordinary amount of discomfort. My psoas are constantly contracting in the area, often my whole body, buzzes and rushes with real ferocity at times. It's pretty much just raw sensation with no emotional component except for frustration. My mind is very obsessive too, and I'm getting more bewildered as the days go on because I'm still not sure what I'm supposed to be doing.

blocks.p: Of course, I can't tell anyone what to do. This isn't therapy. And if it's purely a physical issue, that's out of my scope of practice and expertise. If it's a physical issue by itself, you're probably best to see a doctor.

blocks.h: How I work: from the top of the funnel down

blocks.p: As a therapist, I work from the behavioral domain down to the emotional and cognitive, and further. Think of it as layers, or a funnel:

Usually therapists stick with the emotional, the cognitive and the behavioral. Every now and then they'll incorporate the spiritual. I'm an atheist, so I don't do a whole lot with that. Therapists who are more into the somatic pieces of what makes us us will seek out further training or do their own research and learn more about sensations and impulses. From what I know of Somatic Experiencing, SE practitioners should be able to do that pretty well. It's something I've researched on my own.

Sensation and impulse are really where I hope to get with people, especially when it comes to stuck trauma, a stuck defensive state. We don't have to, but when it comes to really getting unstuck from trauma, I think those domains are pretty darn important.

Mental health therapists aren't trained in physical issues, though. Those could be, or should be, handled by a physical therapist, or a doctor. Coming to a therapist and saying, "I'm having this physical issue," probably won't get you super far, except for a referral to somebody more appropriate. A Reiki practitioner works with the body as well, so that might be more appropriate if you're into that holistic kind of stuff. I don't know much more about it, or whether they can start from the physical.

But even though I may not be able to start from the physical, like a muscle issue, I could definitely work with frustration. Therapists should be able to work from the emotional domain, and then work from there.

Say someone tells me, "I feel lethargy, no energy in my body, but there's no emotional component. At the same time, I feel worthless, and I don't feel pleasure, because I have no motivation and I'm lethargic." To me, the lethargy is more physical: no physical drive in the body. But there's an emotional component too.

The way I work as a therapist is to ask: what came first? I often spend a good amount of time, definitely in my initial assessment, or when panic attacks or relapses come up, doing a chain analysis. What happened first? What happened before that? As best as you can remember. That gives us a clearer picture of what's going on in that moment.

If someone attributes their worthlessness to the lethargy, that could be true, sure. But I could also see someone feeling worthless and feeling lethargy at the same time, with both stemming from a defensive state that's more of a shutdown.

The point is that it's easy for us to say this came first and then that, but we may not know. Even though we know ourselves best, we're not exactly objective about our own experiences. A lot of times in therapy, someone will say, "I think this way, therefore I feel that way." But we know from the "story follows state" concept of Polyvagal Theory that, yes, these things feed into each other, but there's a polyvagal state influencing the cognitions.

So I think it's more accurate to say there's some defensive state affecting the thoughts in our brain. And yes, the thoughts in our brain can influence our emotions, or our state, as well. But people typically can't say, "My thoughts are being flavored by the emotion I'm going through, which is being flavored by the polyvagal state I'm in, and by my incomplete impulses and the sensations I'm living with." We usually can't parse things out like that. So "this comes first, and then I do this" might not be accurate. It could be. That's why I like to do a chain analysis, to see how things flow. It gives me a lot of information as a therapist.

The comment mentioned frustration. Frustration is an emotion, and I think it's a direct, emotional experience of a defensive state. When I feel frustrated, and when I notice it in other people, there's some flight or fight energy. There's energy to do something. We have mobility in our system, and that mobility is being directed toward a task. Maybe that's finishing a level in a video game. Maybe it's completing something at work, or trying to communicate. It could be all kinds of stuff.

Then we're stopped from completing the goal, or we simply can't complete it for some reason. That's frustration: you're mobile, you're ready to do something, you're trying to do it, maybe you've made a plan, but you're stopped. You can't use your mobility toward that goal.

Actually, as I was recording this, I was feeling some frustration. I was mobile and wanted to record in silence. I was trying to sneak in some time, and then there was a commotion across the street, people blowing leaves around. Then it started raining on top of the noise. So I allowed myself to feel my frustration and kept using my mobilization energy to complete the task, because I really wanted you to hear this.

So be careful when attributing thoughts and emotions. I pay particular attention to the sequences of the [SSIEC](piece:snb154-ssiec-state-sensation-impulse-emotion-cognition) domains. What's actually happening when I'm going through something, or when my client is? What's happening now? What came before? And what came before that? I think that's extremely important.

blocks.h: "Activate and relax at the same time"

blocks.p: The next part of the comment:

q: I've had therapists try to get me to further activate my system whilst also asking me to relax. And at this point, I'm confused as hell and exhausted because the activation and discomfort have really wrecked my sleep. I'm very depleted of resources, and I can't stop the activation, which I really need to happen so I can rest properly.

blocks.p: That's not the way I work. I'm a therapist with somatic interventions built into what I do. I'm not a full-on somatic therapist. I blend in CBT. I often blend in solution-focused work. And I blend in a lot of somatic elements. I don't want to assume this is some other modality, but I don't work this way.

I start with where my client is in the moment, not where they want to be or where I want them to be. Of course, we have a goal for therapy that we've created and agreed on: a behavior we want to address, a reduction in one emotion or an increase in another, a reduction in a thought. But no matter where someone is when they come in, with dysregulation or without, that's where we start.

I'm not going to focus on a single body part or a pain and work on that. I'm typically going to start more with emotional or cognitive content and work inward. I work broad, and then narrow it down as the session goes on, down that funnel. And I'm focusing on grounding and safety throughout the session. That might look like me asking, "How are you feeling right now? Do we need to do some grounding?" Or they come in dysregulated, and we do grounding right off the bat, and then work on whatever we're going to work on.

In the back of my mind, the priority is always safety. If they're not in their safety state, or don't have access to it, not a whole lot of good can be done as far as progressing on the treatment plan goal.
So I'm not trying to activate my clients, and I'm also not trying to get them to relax. I don't have a goal of speeding them up or slowing them down. I'm just meeting them where they're at.

They're probably already more active or more relaxed. They already have some flavor of mobility, immobility, or safety in their system. So my goal as a provider is: can I attune to that first? Can I meet them where they're at while staying anchored in my safety state? Can I co-regulate with them? You could call that mirroring on some level. But basically, can I attune, and meet them where they're at, while staying regulated? If I can do that, self-regulation and co-regulation kind of take over from there. Not 100%, but in large part, a lot of good can be done from me attuning to my client and co-regulating with them, and from their own self-regulation in the midst of that.

As this process unfolds, we mindfully experience and witness it, while always staying anchored in our safety state and monitoring our systems for too much dysregulation. For me, that means monitoring my own state; I don't announce what I'm feeling. For the client, I'm prompting them to look inward and notice how much safety they have in their system, if we're using polyvagal language, or more general language that means the same thing.

I had a session recently where I asked a question that was too broad, and my client was insightful enough to recognize they'd just had a big spike of anxiety. They made a motion with their hand, above their head, like a big spike. And I said, "Oh, cool. Thank you so much for recognizing that. Let's whittle this down. Let's get more specific."

There's more to it, of course. I use other therapeutic interventions and techniques along with this. But that's the basic idea when someone comes into the room. I'm not trying to get them to do something, exactly.
If I try to activate someone who's in a dominant dorsal state, it's probably going to fail. I need to be with them. I need to meet them in dorsal while staying anchored in my safety state first.

If I try to relax somebody who's in flight or fight, it's probably going to fail. I need to be with them first. Sometimes I'll ask clients, just to assess in the moment, "Are you able to breathe into your belly? Can you take a deep breath in? Can you extend it slowly?" Someone in flight or fight can't really do that, or it's painful. We can kind of laugh at it, and that actually helps to regulate. But if I insist on them slowing down, it may not be super helpful. If I can meet them where they're at and provide basic therapy skills, normalization, validation, unconditional positive regard, that can help them slow down naturally. Then we can start other therapeutic work.

If someone comes in panicky or in a rage, a dysregulated freeze state, I probably can't slow them down. I don't have the power to do that. What I do is match their energy while staying anchored in my safety state. I don't mean I'm dysregulated with them, or running out of the room. I mean I stay anchored in my safety state, and I get up with them. I can move around with them. We can take a walk outside. I can talk a little higher with them, not dominant, just meeting them where they're at. That's a lot different from someone coming in dysregulated and panicky while I whisper, "Hey, calm down. It's okay. You're okay." That would drive me personally up the wall.

So I don't think trying to get someone somewhere they're not is helpful. My priority is to first meet them, stay anchored in my safety state, and provide co-regulation. As they start to receive the co-regulation and even start to self-regulate, we can be more proactive: "Are you ready to take that deep breath into your belly now? Let's try that and see where you're at." Or, "Which of my fidgets in the room is pulling you toward it? What feels right?" And we work from there.

So if the provider you're with, no matter who they are, therapist or SE practitioner or whatever, is trying to get you to be somewhere you're not, co-regulation might be lacking. I don't know. But they might be coming from their own dysregulated state and trying to fix the problem. Trying to fix you, or your emotions, rather than saying, "You have your emotions. Let me be there with you while I stay anchored. I'll meet you there." That's acting more as an emotional container. If they're trying to get you somewhere you're not, there might be some misattunement, and that's not co-regulation.

I don't try to actively work someone up their ladder through techniques, at least not while they're dysregulated. I meet them where they're at. As they become more regulated, we can be more proactive about further ladder climbing. In times when I've tried to implement something I thought would help, with someone who wasn't able to receive it, it hasn't been helpful.

So do we speed up a client, or relax them? I'd say let's just start with where you're at. That's the starting point. Can I understand what you're going through? Can I feel what you're going through, in my own way? It's not going to be the same. Can I have empathy? Can I feel your true experience right now, without judging it, without trying to change it? Can I just be there with you? That's where I start.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.h: What helps someone enter their safety state

blocks.p: Ask yourself this, especially if you're a provider, or if you're in your own therapy or working with an SE practitioner: what helps someone enter their safety state?

ul: A safe environment. The environment we're in should be safe enough.
Safe people. We can't be being attacked or judged.
Co-regulation. Understanding, being listened to, not being judged. This is all the basic therapy stuff that we therapists should be absolutely nailing.
Mindfulness of the present moment. To have mindfulness, you have to have some safety in your system already, but then you build on that, and on what's happening within you in the present moment.

blocks.p: The goal of therapy is not to speed someone up or slow them down. Besides the treatment plan goal, session to session, the goal is: can we access our safety state? Great. From there, can we access some stuck defensive state energy? Can we titrate and pendulate through that? I wouldn't call that speeding up or slowing down. The priority is safety. And from safety, can we feel into your defensive state, if we're working on stuck trauma?

Sometimes people come in and just want to work on their biggest issue: "I need help dealing with this this week," or "I need to work on boundaries." So what I've laid out here is more specific to trauma, to your stuck state.
The comment finishes:

q: I feel like I've been told that you need to discharge this energy in order to relax, but you won't be able to discharge this energy until you learn to relax.

blocks.p: That makes a lot of sense, because it seems conflicting. If that's what you're being told, yeah, that's confusing. And if you're leaving a session confused, I think that's a problem. It's really important to have clarity on what you're doing in session, and also on what to do after the session to build on it.

As a client in therapy, I want to empower you to ask, "What does that mean? How does that make sense?" If the therapist can't answer it, that's a red flag in my opinion. I pride myself on being able to answer everything my client asks. If I'm implementing something and I can't explain why, that's a problem for me, and a red flag for the client to pick up on. That doesn't really come up for me. I don't make stuff up, and I don't try something I don't understand.

"We need to speed you up and slow you down" is a behavioral, very shallow, top-of-the-funnel understanding. "We need to make you do this. We need to make you do that." If that's all you're getting, that doesn't seem to be cutting the mustard for me. It's like telling someone in a panic attack, "You just need to calm down." Or students at the school where I work: they get angry, leave the classroom, and run through the parking lot. We can tell them, "Stop it," of course. We can tell them, "Dude, take a deep breath, calm down." It doesn't mean we don't say it. But they're just not quite there to accept it. That's a very behavioral "just stop doing that."

So that's how I read the dichotomy of "you need to discharge this energy in order to relax, but you won't be able to discharge this energy until you learn to relax." I think it's a very shallow understanding of all this. And if they can't explain further in session, that's a red flag.

blocks.h: The answer: you need your safety state, not exactly relaxation

blocks.p: I'm going to muddy the water a little bit, and hopefully it makes more sense. You don't need to relax, exactly. You need to activate the body's safety state, so the vagal brake is active, which then allows defensive states to shift.
So do you need to relax in order to discharge your trauma? Behaviorally, that's kind of what it looks like:

ol: You need to be able to be in your safety state.
When your safety state's active, your vagal brake is on.
When your vagal brake is on, your heart beats at a calmer pace.
If your heart beats at a calmer pace, you're going to look more relaxed. You'll be able to exist in stillness, the mixed polyvagal state.

blocks.p: So telling someone "you need to relax" is the very behavioral, top-of-the-funnel way of saying what I just said. I'm hoping that's what they mean, if they have polyvagal knowledge. That's really it: we have to get that safety state active.

Once the safety state is active, you'll be able to exist in stillness and be more mindful of what's happening inside of you. If you can do that and tap into your stuck defensive state, you'll probably notice more energy coming into your system. Depending on the flavor of what's happening inside of you, you'll probably notice that stuck defensive state energy surfacing, and you'll become more mobilized.
Irene Lyon described this when she was on the podcast:

q: The moment the safety comes up, what does it allow the system to do? It allows it to express all the stored stuff that has been in there forever…

blocks.p: If you're coming out of shutdown up into fight, you're going to feel more aggression. You're going to feel that power come into your system, and we want the vagal brake to be active so you can tolerate it.

If you're coming out of a freeze state, you're going to notice some fear, and you'll have to be able to sit with the immobility of fear and the stuck flight and fight energy of fear. But the way I work, I don't want to go there with my client until I know their vagal brake can handle it, because I don't want to re-traumatize them. So telling someone, "Speed up," might not be helpful. It might be re-traumatizing, depending on how it looks.

Maybe that's what these three SE practitioners were trying to accomplish: get you to anchor in safety and then feel into your stuck defensive state. I don't know. That's the brightest possible way of looking at it. But they should be able to explain what the hell they're doing. If they're not, that's a problem.

If you just tell someone, "Let's speed up," you're just giving advice. Anybody can do that. "Just slow down and relax," or "You've got to relax first so you can feel your pain." Okay, that's not super helpful unless you can actually do the steps required to help that person get there, and you've got to be able to explain it.

I think that's very shallow advice. I don't think it has an understanding of what's actually happening, and I don't think it necessarily involves co-regulation. You can definitely co-regulate with somebody by connecting with them and explaining the significance of anchoring in safety and slowing down, so they can actually feel their defensive state mindfully. Sure. But you can also be really misattuned and disconnected from someone and tell them, "You've got to speed up," or "You've got to slow down." That's not co-regulation. That's advice-giving, and it's not really connecting with someone.

Maybe you're thinking, "Well, no, it's different in my case, because..." Okay, fine. In general, that's what I'm arguing. You need to be able to explain how, and you need to be able to connect with the people you're working with.
